name: Training Datasets
blurb: Corpora used to pre-train models, with provenance and licence.

items.note: Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus; trained T5 and remains the most-downloaded classic pretraining set
15 trillion tokens of filtered CommonCrawl; the reference open web-scale pretraining corpus
The education-filtered FineWeb subset that lifted small-model benchmarks and set the quality-over-quantity pattern
The largest fully open corpus built from public-domain and permissioned text only
6TB of permissively-licensed source code behind StarCoder; gated with an opt-out process for authors
The 825GB corpus that defined open pretraining data in the GPT-Neo era; historically important, now superseded
AI2's 3-trillion-token corpus with full documentation of what went in and why; trained the OLMo models
Open reproduction of the LLaMA training mix

reading.body:
C4 remains the most-downloaded pretraining corpus in this set by a factor of three over its nearest competitor, which says something about the weight of incumbency in training data even as newer, larger alternatives exist.

The eight datasets here span roughly three generations of open pretraining practice. The Pile defined what open pretraining data looked like in the GPT-Neo era, C4 and RedPajama followed as filtered and reproducible alternatives, and FineWeb and Dolma represent the current generation, which prioritises documented provenance and licence clarity alongside scale. FineWeb-edu's download count, nearly as high as FineWeb itself despite being a filtered subset, reflects a shift in practitioner thinking: a smaller, higher-quality corpus can outperform a larger one on benchmark tasks, and the community has absorbed that lesson quickly. For AI training specifically, this matters because data quality affects how much compute is needed to reach a given capability level, and wasted compute means wasted power and time in the data centre.

Six of the eight datasets carry explicit open licences, either ODC-BY or a named alternative, and none of the six are gated. The Stack is the outlier: gated, with a non-standard licence and an author opt-out process, reflecting the particular legal sensitivity around code. Common Corpus and RedPajama both lack a recorded licence in this data, which is a gap a practitioner would need to resolve before use. The data covers downloads and licences but not dataset ages, versioning history, or how each corpus has been used in production training runs, so it cannot answer questions about which corpora are actually inside the models most widely deployed today.
